claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units narrowly, limiting increases and extending tenure security but not capping rent levels.
SDU tenants pay a 15–25 percent per-square-foot premium because their options are exhausted, and they are disproportionately vulnerable groups.
The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance capped increases within tenancies but left initial rents untouched and excluded co-living SDUs.
Mrs Wong, a nine-year SDU tenant without a written agreement, says the ordinance changed nothing she can see.
A 10 percent rent cut caused by a cap removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of marginal housing stock over five years.
The landlords association argues a hard initial-rent cap is confiscatory and promises members will leave the segment if returns fall below mortgage cost.
The landlords association admits it has no data on members' real margins, and its compliance-cost figures come from a self-reported survey with only a 34 percent response rate.
Hard caps on rent levels show consistent stock contraction, while caps on increases within tenancies show small or null effects on stock.
The stability of SDU stock since 2021 is not proof that binding caps are safe because the 2021 ordinance is second-generation and non-binding.
One think-tank's inference that stable stock proves capacity for more control misreads the natural experiment.
Median rent per square foot in subdivided units rose 3.1 percent from 2021 to 2023, faster than the 1.7 percent for general private rent.
The rent burden for SDU households worsened from 31 to 34 percent of income over the same period.
An NGO survey of 440 households found that 61 percent would trade a rent increase for three years of security of tenure, and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer.
The NGO report says the real problem is a long queue, and rent caps treat the price symptom of a quantity problem.
The NGO report supports a narrow tightening with tenure security and a light band on initial rents, and opposes a hard cap.
A light, indexed band on initial rents is legally defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation, surviving judicial review.
Current inspection covers under 6 percent of stock annually, and a certifiable tenancy register needs 40–60 staff-years.
The subcommittee could not design an enforcement model that protects the newest-arrival tail first rather than last.
The queue will not shorten this decade, and tenants are being harmed now, so 'don't cap, fix supply' is not a complete answer.
The defensible position is a narrow tightening: tenure security, a reviewable initial-rent band, and enforcement investment targeted at the most exploited tail.
